                    ### Question
                    A 25-year-old woman presented to an urgent care center with a complaint of a cough for more than 3 weeks that was accompanied by night sweats, weight loss, and malaise. On physical examination, the patient had slightly pale palpebral conjunctivae bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, but with no adventitious breath sounds in the lung fields bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was routine. The patient was started on a drug regimen that was to be taken for 6 months. On follow-up after 2 months, the ALT and AST levels were elevated. Which of the following anti-tubercular drug could have contributed to this labor result?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rifampicin
opb. Pyrazinamide
opc. Isoniazid
opd. Streptomycin
ope. Ethambutol

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Among the anti-tubercular drugs, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are strongly associated with hepatotoxic effects, which can lead to elevated ALT and AST levels. Isoniazid is a common cause of drug-induced liver injury in tuberculosis treatment. Pyrazinamide is also known for its significant hepatotoxicity. Rifampicin can mildly elevate liver enzymes but is generally less implicated compared to isoniazid and pyrazinamide. Streptomycin and ethambutol, known for causing nephrotoxicity and optic neuritis respectively, are unlikely to cause elevated liver enzymes.
